title: Monetary Policy Report—April 2025
summary: The Bank of Canada published its April 2025 Monetary Policy Report maintaining the overnight rate target at 2.75%, with the Bank Rate at 3% and deposit rate at 2.70%. The report notes that while inflation was near the 2% target at end-2024 and rate cuts had bolstered growth, escalating US tariffs and trade uncertainty are now diminishing growth prospects and adding price pressures. Removing the consumer carbon tax will temporarily lower inflation, including a one-time reduction in consumer prices driven largely by declining gasoline prices.
key_points: Bank of Canada held policy rate at 2.75% (overnight rate target), with Bank Rate at 3% and deposit rate at 2.70%
Inflation was near the 2% target in Q4 2024 following prior interest rate cuts
US has threatened, imposed, and suspended tariffs on Canada, creating highly uncertain trade outlook
Trade uncertainty and tariffs are expected to slow economic growth and add to price pressures
Canada's potential output growth anticipated to slow due to declining population growth and ongoing trade conflict
Canada's neutral interest rate range is estimated between 2.25% and 3.25%
why_it_matters: This quarterly policy report provides the Bank of Canada's official assessment of the Canadian economy and its outlook. With the US threatening and implementing tariffs on Canadian goods, the report signals that trade conflict is now the dominant risk factor suppressing growth while simultaneously threatening to increase inflation—creating a stagflationary risk dynamic. Market participants use these reports to gauge the BoC's reaction function and policy path under uncertainty.
macro_context: The BoC faces a challenging environment where tariffs raise inflation while trade uncertainty depresses growth—a classic stagflationary mix. The neutral rate range of 2.25%–3.25% provides context for where policy rates would settle if the economy were at equilibrium. The report highlights that the removal of the consumer carbon tax creates a one-time downward shift in the price level, complicating interpretation of underlying inflation trends.
